content: Infantile colic is a prevalent condition, affecting approximately one in six families. In 2001, it was estimated to cost the UK National Health Service over £65 million annually. Although colic typically resolves by six months of age, there is evidence suggesting potential long-term consequences for both children and their parents. Manipulative therapies, including chiropractic, osteopathy, and cranial manipulation, have been proposed as potential treatments to alleviate the symptoms of infantile colic. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and effectiveness of manipulative therapies for treating infantile colic in infants under six months of age. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and others, covering literature up to April 2012. Additional searches were performed in specialized databases, and over 90 chiropractic and osteopathic institutions worldwide were contacted. Randomized trials evaluating the effects of chiropractic, osteopathy, or cranial osteopathy, either alone or in combination with other interventions, were included in the review. The review identified six studies involving a total of 325 infants. Three additional studies were identified but lacked sufficient information, and three more were ongoing at the time of the review. Of the six included studies, five suggested a beneficial effect of manipulative therapies, while one found no evidence of benefit. When data from five studies measuring daily crying hours were combined, manipulative therapies were associated with a significant reduction in crying time, averaging 1 hour and 12 minutes less per day (mean difference: -1.20 hours; 95% confidence interval: -1.89 to -0.51). This finding remained consistent when considering studies with a low risk of selection bias, attrition bias, or those published in peer-reviewed journals. However, when only studies with a low risk of performance bias (i.e., parental blinding) were analyzed, the reduction in crying hours was not statistically significant (mean difference: -0.57 hours; 95% confidence interval: -2.24 to 1.09). One study evaluated whether the reduction in crying time was clinically significant. It found that a higher proportion of parents whose infants received manipulative therapy reported clinically significant improvements compared to parents of untreated infants. Specifically, the odds of reducing crying to less than two hours per day were significantly higher (odds ratio: 6.33; 95% confidence interval: 1.54 to 26.00), as were the odds of achieving a reduction in crying by more than 30% (odds ratio: 3.70; 95% confidence interval: 1.15 to 11.86). However, data from three studies assessing full recovery from colic, as reported by parents, did not show a statistically significant difference between infants receiving manipulative therapies and those who did not (odds ratio: 11.12; 95% confidence interval: 0.46 to 267.52). One study measured infant sleep duration and found that manipulative therapy led to a statistically significant improvement in sleep time (mean difference: 1.17 hours; 95% confidence interval: 0.22 to 2.12). The quality of the included studies varied. While there was generally a low risk of selection bias, only two studies were deemed to have a low risk of performance bias, three had a low risk of detection bias, and one had a low risk of attrition bias. Only one study reported on adverse events, and no adverse events were observed. However, the small sample size of 325 infants limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions about the safety of these interventions. In conclusion, the studies included in this review were generally small and methodologically prone to bias, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of manipulative therapies for infantile colic. Most studies suggested that parents of infants receiving manipulative therapies reported fewer hours of crying per day, and this reduction was statistically significant. Additionally, a greater proportion of parents reported clinically significant improvements. However, the high risk of performance bias, due to the lack of blinding among parents, limits the reliability of these findings. When only studies with a low risk of performance bias were considered, the results were not statistically significant. Further research is needed, particularly studies where outcome assessors are blinded to the treatment allocation. There is also insufficient data to make definitive conclusions about the safety of manipulative therapies for infantile colic.
